message.reasoning:
I need to make a Monopoly decision.

Only one opponent remains. I have $935 and am on Mediterranean Avenue. I'm checking which properties are mortgaged and what color groups I control.

I own the red group with houses on Indiana and Illinois. I hold the orange monopoly but all three properties are mortgaged. I also have a mortgaged B&O railroad.

I also own Ventnor, Pennsylvania Avenue, and Short Line. Park Place has a hotel and Boardwalk has four houses.

The opponent owns the brown monopoly with hotels on Mediterranean and Baltic. They also hold Reading Railroad, Oriental Avenue, St. Charles, Electric Company, Virginia, Pennsylvania Railroad, Water Works, Marvin Gardens, Pacific, and North Carolina.

Atlantic Avenue is unowned.

I passed GO and paid $250 rent on Mediterranean, leaving me with $935. I can trade with the opponent, unmortgage properties, or build houses on Kentucky and Boardwalk.

The opponent has $563 and sits on Baltic Avenue. I am calculating whether my Park Place hotel rent of $1,500 or Boardwalk four houses at $1,700 can bankrupt them.

Selling a hotel returns half its cost, which equals one house. To fully liquidate the opponent's brown hotels, I would need to sell both hotels and then sell all four houses on each property.

Selling both brown hotels returns only $250. I am now checking mortgage values for the opponent's remaining properties to gauge liquidation.

The opponent's total liquidation value is roughly $1,793. Park Place hotel rent of $1,500 and Boardwalk four houses at $1,700 are both survivable. A Boardwalk hotel at $2,000 would bankrupt them. Building a hotel on Boardwalk is the only viable kill shot.

Building a hotel on Boardwalk costs $200. That leaves me with $735 after construction. The bank has enough houses and hotels to cover this. The uneven building requirement is satisfied because Park Place already has a hotel and Boardwalk four houses.

Building a house on Kentucky would cost $150 and raise its rent to $250. That is not enough to bankrupt the opponent, so I will focus on Boardwalk.

I confirmed that maxing out the red group would only yield about $750 in rent, which is still too low to bankrupt the opponent. The Boardwalk hotel remains the sole viable kill shot.

I will build the Boardwalk hotel now. It costs $200 and turns the square into a guaranteed bankruptcy trap. The opponent can survive four houses at $1,700 but cannot afford a hotel at $2,000. I am on Mediterranean Avenue and ready to roll.

I am mapping the opponent's possible landing spots from Baltic Avenue. A roll of 3 lands on Income Tax, while a roll of 22 lands on Indiana Avenue. I need to see which squares they might reach.

I mapped the opponent's possible landing spots from Baltic Avenue. A roll of 2 through 14 lands on Reading, Oriental, Vermont, Connecticut, Jail, St. Charles, Electric, Virginia, or Pennsylvania Railroad. None of these squares are Park Place, Boardwalk, or my red properties. The opponent cannot land on those squares from this position.

Building the Boardwalk hotel is a long-term play. The opponent cannot land on my developed properties next turn unless they draw a Chance card. I have enough cash to afford the $200 construction. I am also checking whether I might land on their hotels myself.

I am checking whether I might land on their utilities. If I roll a 10 to reach Electric Company, the rent would be $100. Their St. Charles is mortgaged and worth nothing. Virginia is not a monopoly for them.

The worst ordinary rent I could face next turn is about $200, which I can easily afford. I will not land on Baltic this roll because I have already passed it. Building the Boardwalk hotel would give me five total houses and two hotels, so any future repairs from Chance or Community Chest cards would be costly.

I calculated the repair costs for five houses and two hotels. General repairs cost $325 and street repairs cost $430, both well within my remaining cash. I am now weighing whether to unmortgage the orange monopoly properties.

Unmortgaging the orange set costs $308. Even fully developed, the orange properties would not bankrupt the opponent. The highest rent is only about $600, which is still below their liquidation value of roughly $1,793. Building on the orange group is not a viable kill shot.

I lack monopolies on the pink, yellow, and green groups. Unmortgaging my railroads would only yield $50 in rent, so that is not worthwhile either. I will keep all cash for the Boardwalk hotel and as a buffer against their brown hotels and future repairs. I am now considering whether to trade.

I ruled out any trade that would help the opponent survive the Boardwalk hotel. Giving them cash or a green monopoly would only strengthen their position. The pink group is also not worth trading for, since its highest rent is still below their liquidation value and would increase their survival odds.

Green properties are too dangerous to trade for. Even one house on the green monopoly would cost over $1,000 in rent, which exceeds my remaining cash of $735. I will not give them the green set. I am proceeding with the Boardwalk hotel build.

The hotel count is one. Boardwalk qualifies for the upgrade and is legal to build. I will skip adding a house to Kentucky to preserve cash. I plan to post a short, confident public message about upgrading Boardwalk.

The opponent's unmortgaged properties total $980. I am verifying the official rule that hotels sell back to the bank for half their original cost.

I confirmed the official rule: selling a hotel returns half its purchase price plus four houses. Each brown hotel costs $50, so selling both brown hotels would return $250 in cash and four houses. The bank currently holds 23 houses, so it can easily provide them.
